title: Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI
abstract: Last year, we introduced GEM , the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions. The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for. GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers. GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas: 1. Bending the Scaling Curve, Enabling 2.5x Model Complexity Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions. Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun , co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results. 2. Efficient Intelligence Transfer From GEM to User-Facing Models Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI. Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM , a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation ( Solaris ) to harvest the gains from the upstream model. 3. Accelerating the Central Compute Engine With Large-Scale Cross-Surface, Cross-Domain Learning at Meta Ads Scale Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously. Solution: GEM accelerates one single, unified compute engine through the central foundation model that jointly predicts clicks and conversions across all surfaces, including Facebook and Instagram, and acro

title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains. Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations. In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example. Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle. This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid. This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation: A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N] Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension. During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout: Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096). Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192). Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization. In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. title: CASTLE: training natural language search before the first real query
abstract: How we addressed the cold-start problem for Airbnb’s natural language search by jointly generating synthetic training data — queries and relevance labels — from de-identified booking and search signals. By : Wendy Ran Wei , Hao Li , Weiwei Guo , Xiaowei Liu , Xueyin Chen , Chun How Tan , Malay Haldar , Soumyadip Banerjee , Kedar Bellare , Huiji Gao , Sanjeev Katariya , and Stephanie Moyerman Introduction Natural language search lets guests express intent in their own words, such as “romantic cabin near skiing” or “pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight,” rather than navigating filters and categories. We needed to introduce this kind of search for Airbnb, and to have it work well from the start. However, this required training the model before we had actual user queries to train the model on, and a reasonable set of relevance labels (inferred from the queries) to map queries to matching listings. Without prior traffic, both must be synthesized from scratch. This is the cold-start problem for natural-language search. Other organizations have faced similar challenges and have created methods to address them. However, prior approaches address the need for a body of queries and the need for relevance labels separately. Passage-based methods such as InPars [1] prompt a large language model (LLM) to generate queries conditioned on a single document, then rely on additional LLM judgments to assign relevance labels, introducing a second source of error. Promptagator [2] improves query diversity using few-shot examples, but is still limited by the gap between its generation distribution and real user behavior. In this post, we describe Contrastive And Seed-guided Training for natural Language sEarch (CASTLE), our framework for jointly generating queries and producing relevance labels from Airbnb’s own de-identified booking data. Our paper describing CASTLE was accepted as a full research paper at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, more widely known as CIKM 2026 [3]. Challenges Generating useful synthetic training data for search requires more than producing grammatically plausible queries. The distribution of synthetic queries must match how real guests actually search; their preferred phrasing, query length, and attributes they tend to mention. If queries fail to match real-world search patterns, the model trained on them will generalize poorly. We measured this mismatch using Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (a measure of how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution) between synthetic and real query distributions — both over surface-level query statistics and over attribute types (property type, amenity, location, and so on). Prior approaches scored between 9.33 and 26.2 on the KL divergence metric: far from the real-user distribution. Beyond distributional alignment, we also needed relevance labels. Generating a query is only half the problem; knowing which listings are relevant to it is the other half. Solution CASTLE addresses both challenges through a single mechanism: contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions, selected in accordance with user privacy permissions. When a guest books a specific listing after viewing several possible alternatives, that event implicitly encodes preference: the booked listing was selected over the others. We use these (positive, negative) pairs of listings — where the negative is randomly sampled from the other viewed-but-not-booked alternatives — as the structured input for query generation. Listing features include amenities, property details, and a one sentence summary of recent public guest reviews, with personal identifying information removed. Because we instruct the LLM to generate a query that is satisfied by the positive listing but not the negative, the relevance label is correct by construction; no post-hoc judgment is required. title: Mix, Don't Tune: Bilingual Pre-Training Outperforms Hyperparameter Search in Data-Constrained Settings
abstract: For most languages of the world, language model pre-training operates in a data-constrained regime where models must repeat their training data many times, degrading generalization. Two remedies exist: aggressive hyperparameter tuning such as high weight decay, and mixing in data from a high-resource auxiliary language to directly aid the low-resource target. While hyperparameter tuning regularizes the model by shrinking weights to restrict network capacity, auxiliary data mixing uses a tunable mixing ratio to expand the training distribution and diversify the training signal with new…

title: Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements
abstract: Managing AI model access across dozens or hundreds of AWS accounts creates operational friction when each workload account must subscribe and accept AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers (MPPOs) individually. Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements simplifies multi-account access to third-party AI models so you can subscribe once from a central account and distribute access across your organization. In this post, we show you two ways to activate AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offer (MPPO) entitlements in AWS License Manager. Use the lightweight script when you want a one-time, no-infrastructure fix for received licenses you already trust. Use the CDK automation when you want ongoing event-driven processing that verifies sellers, creates and activates distributed grants. Why automate grant activation With AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers, you can negotiate custom rates for third-party models on Amazon Bedrock. After an eligible private offer is accepted, AWS Marketplace creates a license in AWS License Manager. In AWS Organizations with all features enabled, organization-level grants are auto-accepted but remain Disabled until you activate them. Teams often manage this by checking the AWS License Manager console and activating grants manually. Manual checks work, but they add effort and are easy to miss. Until someone activates the grant, negotiated pricing does not apply. The same effort appears as teams adopt new models or renew terms. Solution overview The sample repository provides two paths: Path 1 – The lightweight path is a standalone script that lists received licenses and prints a dry-run plan. It only creates and activates organization-wide grants when you re-run it with --apply --confirm-account-id . It has no seller allow-list, so use it only when you trust every received license in the management account. Path 2 – The event-driven path uses AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy ongoing automation in your AWS management account. Choose one of the following implementation paths. Use Path 1 for one-time activation without CDK. Use Path 2 for ongoing event-driven automation. Path 1: Lightweight script (one-time activation) Use this path when you need one-time activation without deploying CDK. The script lists every received license in the management account, so use the dry run as your review gate before applying changes. Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements.git cd sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements Run the lightweight script in dry-run mode. python3 lightweight/distribute_licenses.py Review every listed license and confirm that the ISV Partner issuer and account scope match the private offer you expect. Apply the reviewed plan from the same AWS Organizations management account. python3 lightweight/distribute_licenses.py --apply --confirm-account-id ACCOUNT_ID After the grant is active, validate the billing path before you rely on the private offer in production. Billing data in AWS Cost Explorer can lag, so use it to compare the effective charge for covered Amazon Bedrock usage after charges appear. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and confirm the expected discount path. Path 2: CDK automation (ongoing activation) Use this path when you want new private pricing agreements handled automatically. The CDK stack listens for eligible AWS Marketplace agreement events, checks your seller allowlist, creates distributed grants, and retries activation when License Manager needs more time. The solution contains three components: Amazon EventBridge rule : The stack listens for AWS Marketplace agreement events on the default event bus in us-east-1 . title: WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with spatial, embodied, physical, and temporal reasoning. We hypothesize that these failures reflect a shared deficit in visual transition reasoning, and test whether this capability can serve as a shared training primitive, one that different models can learn from different supervision sources and reuse across different tasks, with a systematic training recipe. Existing benchmarks document these deficits separately but do not support controlled comparisons across scenes, actions, and reasoning operations. We therefore introduce WOVEN, a training source and benchmark for visual transition reasoning that organizes transition supervision by scene, action, and reasoning type, using diverse, realistic rollouts from video-pretrained generative models: 36,076 examples across 20 scene types, 5 action types, and 8 reasoning types. We first evaluate 38 frontier MLLMs (e.g., GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B) and find a substantial and systematic deficit: even the strongest models fall far below humans, and the failures recur across model families and persist with scale. We then train MLLMs at multiple scales on WOVEN and find that they learn a shared capability that transfers broadly: training subsets of only about 2,000 items each collectively improve 22 of 26 external benchmarks by up to 27.3 percentage points, and WOVEN data can replace 30-50% of a task's own training data with comparable accuracy. Controlled comparisons further yield a training recipe for visual world modeling, validated prospectively on held-out benchmarks: select supervision by the reasoning operation it teaches rather than by the actions, scenes, or domains it shows, and prefer larger changes to the visual state for robustness. Our work establishes visual transition reasoning as a reusable foundation for systematic visual world-model training in MLLMs.
